Unit 8 — Hypothesis Testing, Effect Sizes, Power and Multiple Comparisons

A hypothesis test answers one narrow question: could what I am seeing plausibly have been produced by chance alone? It does not say whether the effect matters, whether the experiment was designed correctly, or whether the comparison was decided before or after looking at the data — and most of the damage done by testing in the biomedical and chemical literature comes from reading the answer to the narrow question as an answer to the broad ones. This unit builds testing from a single idea, the permutation test, from which every classical test turns out to be a computational shortcut, and then spends most of its length on the three things that decide whether a test result is worth anything: the effect size with its interval, the multiplicity of the comparisons that were actually made, and the power the design ever had. The centrepiece is an experiment on the laboratory’s own simulation data in which the same comparison yields p = 1.1 × 10−26 and p = 0.69 depending on whether frames or replicas are counted as the experimental unit — and only one of those two numbers is admissible.

Resumen en español

Esta unidad construye las pruebas de hipótesis a partir de una sola idea, la prueba de permutación, y muestra que las pruebas clásicas (t de Student, Welch, pareada, Mann-Whitney, Wilcoxon, ANOVA, Kruskal-Wallis, ji-cuadrado y exacta de Fisher) son atajos de cálculo de esa misma idea, cada uno con sus supuestos. Se explica qué es y qué no es un valor p, su relación con el intervalo de confianza, y se calculan tamaños de efecto con intervalos (d de Cohen, g de Hedges, delta de Cliff, correlación biserial de rangos, razón de momios) con el paquete effectsize. Se aborda el problema de las comparaciones múltiples sobre mil genes de una matriz de expresión con diseño pareado (Bonferroni, Holm y Benjamini-Hochberg a mano y con p.adjust, FWER frente a FDR, valores q), el p-hacking y el jardín de senderos que se bifurcan, la potencia estadística estimada por simulación para 3 y 10 réplicas de dinámica molecular, y la maldición del ganador. El experimento central compara la misma hipótesis evaluada por fotograma y por réplica. Esta es la edición en R; la edición en Python contiene el mismo material.

Learning objectives

  • Formulate a null hypothesis, build its null distribution by permutation, and recognise the classical tests as special cases of that construction.
  • Choose between Student, Welch, paired, Mann–Whitney, Wilcoxon, ANOVA, Kruskal–Wallis, chi-square and Fisher tests, and check the assumptions each one makes.
  • Interpret a p-value correctly, state its relationship to the confidence interval, and explain why “significant” is not “important”.
  • Compute Cohen’s d, Hedges’ g, Cliff’s delta, the rank-biserial correlation and an odds ratio, each with a confidence interval.
  • Correct for multiplicity with Bonferroni, Holm and Benjamini–Hochberg, distinguish family-wise error from false discovery rate, and compute q-values.
  • Recognise p-hacking, the garden of forking paths and HARKing, and write a pre-registered analysis plan for a thesis.
  • Estimate statistical power by simulation, decide how many replicas or compounds an experiment needs, and anticipate the winner’s curse.
  • Identify the experimental unit of a study and avoid pseudoreplication.

How to read this unit

Read linearly, running every chunk; then re-run the permutation chunks with a different seed and watch which conclusions move. Everything runs on base R’s stats[1] plus data.table, ggplot2, Matrix (for the fingerprints), car (Levene’s test) and effectsize[35]; in a fresh Google Colab R runtime run once: install.packages(c(“data.table”,“ggplot2”,“Matrix”,“car”,“effectsize”,“R.utils”)). This unit assumes Unit 7 (sampling distributions, bootstrap, autocorrelation) and feeds Unit 9, where the same tests reappear as questions about regression coefficients. 

suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(data.table); library(ggplot2); library(Matrix); library(car); library(effectsize)
})
set.seed(0)
PAL <- c(blue = "#2b5d9b", orange = "#d2691e", green = "#3a7d44", purple = "#6a4c93")
theme_set(theme_bw(base_size = 9) +
          theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
                plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 10)))
pfmt <- function(p) ifelse(p < 1e-300, "< 1e-300", sprintf("%.3g", p))
cat("R", paste(R.version$major, R.version$minor, sep = "."),
    "| data.table", as.character(packageVersion("data.table")),
    "| Matrix", as.character(packageVersion("Matrix")),
    "| car", as.character(packageVersion("car")),
    "| effectsize", as.character(packageVersion("effectsize")), "\n")
## R 4.5.3 | data.table 1.18.6.1 | Matrix 1.7.5 | car 3.1.5 | effectsize 1.0.3

The helper pfmt exists because R’s t.test returns a p-value of exactly 0 when the true value falls below the smallest representable double (about 10−308); printing “0” in a paper is wrong, and this unit will meet that case twice.

D    <- function(f) file.path("..", "data", f)
rock <- fread(D("rock1_chembl_curated.csv")); exact <- rock[censored == FALSE]
md_obs <- fread(D("md_trpcage_observables.csv"))
expr <- fread(D("geo_periodontitis_expr.csv"))
meta <- fread(D("geo_periodontitis_meta.csv"))
lib  <- fread(D("screening_library.csv"))
cat("ROCK1 compounds with exact potency :", nrow(exact), "\n")
## ROCK1 compounds with exact potency : 2764
cat("MD frames                          :", nrow(md_obs), "=", uniqueN(md_obs$condition),
    "conditions x", uniqueN(md_obs$replica), "replicas x",
    md_obs[, .N, by = .(condition, replica)]$N[1], "frames\n")
## MD frames                          : 3000 = 2 conditions x 3 replicas x 500 frames
cat("expression matrix                  :", nrow(expr), "genes x", ncol(expr) - 1, "samples\n")
## expression matrix                  : 5000 genes x 138 samples
cat("samples                            :", paste(names(table(meta$status)), table(meta$status),
                                                   collapse = ", "),
    "| patients:", uniqueN(meta$patient_id), "\n")
## samples                            : diseased 69, healthy 69 | patients: 69
cat("screening library                  :", nrow(lib), "molecules,", sum(lib$label),
    "actives,", sum(lib$label == 0), "decoys\n")
## screening library                  : 12018 molecules, 1327 actives, 10691 decoys

Four tables, three kinds of comparison: 2,764 compounds with a measured potency, 3,000 simulation frames in six runs, 5,000 genes measured in 138 samples from 69 patients, and a 12,018-molecule screening library with 1,327 known actives.

1. What a test is, and what the laboratory tests

A statistical test has four parts, and writing all four down before computing anything removes most of the confusion:

  1. a null hypothesis \(H_0\) — a complete, simulatable description of “nothing is going on” (the labels carry no information; the two conditions have the same distribution);
  2. a test statistic \(T\) — any number computed from the data that is large when the effect is present (a difference of means, a difference of medians, an area under a ROC curve);
  3. the null distribution — the distribution of \(T\) if \(H_0\) were true, obtained either from a formula or by simulation;
  4. the p-value — the probability, under \(H_0\), of a test statistic at least as extreme as the one observed.

Domain context — the three comparisons this laboratory makes

(a) Actives versus decoys. In virtual screening a computational score ranks a library of molecules; to know whether the score works, it is run on a set of known actives (molecules measured to bind the target) mixed with decoys (molecules assumed inactive, usually chosen to resemble the actives physically but to be structurally different). Our frozen library holds 1,327 ROCK1 actives and 10,691 decoys. The score used below is the maximum Tanimoto similarity of each molecule to a small set of 25 reference actives: the Tanimoto coefficient compares two molecular fingerprints — bit vectors recording which substructures a molecule contains — and ranges from 0 (nothing in common) to 1 (identical fingerprints).

(b) Two simulation conditions. Three replica molecular-dynamics runs at 300 K against three at 340 K, as described in Unit 7: the question is whether the protein is measurably less stable at the higher temperature after 1 ns. A replica is an independent repetition of the same simulation with a different random seed.

(c) Diseased versus healthy tissue. 69 patients each contributed one gingival (gum) tissue sample from a site affected by periodontitis — a chronic inflammatory disease of the tissues around the teeth — and one from a clinically healthy site[2]. Each sample’s RNA was measured on a microarray, giving a log2 expression value for 5,000 genes. Because both samples come from the same patient, the design is paired, and ignoring that pairing throws away most of the information.

2. The permutation test is the whole idea

If the labels are meaningless, then any re-assignment of the labels to the same data is as likely as the one we observed. So: compute the statistic on the real labelling; shuffle the labels many times and recompute; the p-value is the fraction of shuffles that reach or exceed the real value. That is the entire procedure[3]. It makes no assumption about normality, requires no formula, and works for any statistic you can compute — a difference of medians, an enrichment factor, an AUC.

Substitution in the R edition — fingerprints

The Python edition computes Morgan fingerprints with RDKit inside the notebook. R has no RDKit binding in this environment, so the fingerprints (radius 2, 2,048 bits) were generated once with RDKit and frozen as a sparse (id, bit) file, data/screening_morgan_sparse.csv.gz, whose provenance is recorded in data/manifest_fingerprints.json; data/rock1_curated.sdf.gz ships the structures so that a reader with ChemmineR or rcdk can recompute them. Rebuilding the bit matrix with Matrix::sparseMatrix() and computing Tanimoto similarities from it is three lines of sparse algebra, written out in the next chunk. Nothing else in the unit depends on chemistry software. 

fp  <- fread(D("screening_morgan_sparse.csv.gz"))                   ## columns: id, bit (0-based)
M   <- sparseMatrix(i = match(fp$id, lib$inchikey), j = fp$bit + 1L, x = 1,
                    dims = c(nrow(lib), 2048))                      ## molecules x bits
pc  <- rowSums(M)                                                   ## popcount per molecule
set.seed(0)
ref <- sample(which(lib$label == 1), 25)                            ## 25 reference actives
inter <- as.matrix(M %*% t(M[ref, , drop = FALSE]))                 ## |A and B| for every pair
tani  <- inter / (outer(pc, pc[ref], "+") - inter)                   ## |A and B| / |A or B|
score <- apply(tani, 1, max)
keep  <- rep(TRUE, nrow(lib)); keep[ref] <- FALSE                    ## never score a reference on itself
y <- lib$label[keep]; s <- score[keep]
act <- s[y == 1]; dec <- s[y == 0]
cat(sprintf("fingerprint matrix: %d molecules x %d bits, %d set bits (mean %.1f per molecule)\n",
            nrow(M), ncol(M), nrow(fp), mean(pc)))
## fingerprint matrix: 12018 molecules x 2048 bits, 617137 set bits (mean 51.4 per molecule)
cat(sprintf("actives: n = %d, mean score %.3f, median %.3f\n", length(act), mean(act), median(act)))
## actives: n = 1302, mean score 0.438, median 0.442
cat(sprintf("decoys : n = %d, mean score %.3f, median %.3f\n", length(dec), mean(dec), median(dec)))
## decoys : n = 10691, mean score 0.179, median 0.175
cat(sprintf("observed difference of means: %.4f\n", mean(act) - mean(dec)))
## observed difference of means: 0.2594

Each molecule carries on average 51.4 of the 2,048 bits, so the matrix is 2.5 % dense and the whole similarity calculation is one sparse matrix product. The 1,302 actives (25 of the 1,327 are references and were removed) score 0.438 on average against 0.179 for the 10,691 decoys, a raw difference of 0.2594 similarity units. Is that difference bigger than label noise?

permutation_test <- function(a, b, stat = function(x, y) mean(x) - mean(y),
                             n_perm = 5000, seed = 0, alternative = "greater") {
  set.seed(seed)
  pooled <- c(a, b); n_a <- length(a); obs <- stat(a, b)
  null <- replicate(n_perm, { p <- sample(pooled); stat(p[1:n_a], p[(n_a + 1):length(p)]) })
  p_val <- if (alternative == "greater") (1 + sum(null >= obs)) / (n_perm + 1)
           else (1 + sum(abs(null) >= abs(obs))) / (n_perm + 1)      ## the +1 keeps the p-value valid
  list(obs = obs, p = p_val, null = null)
}
r1 <- permutation_test(act, dec, n_perm = 5000, seed = 0)
p <- ggplot(data.frame(null = r1$null), aes(null)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 50, fill = "grey75", colour = NA) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = 3) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(-0.02, 0.28)) +
  annotate("segment", x = r1$obs, xend = r1$obs, y = 0, yend = Inf,
           colour = PAL["orange"], linewidth = 1) +
  annotate("text", x = r1$obs, y = Inf, vjust = 1.6, hjust = 1.05, size = 2.8,
           label = sprintf("observed = %.3f", r1$obs)) +
  labs(x = "difference of mean similarity (actives - decoys) under shuffled labels", y = "count",
       title = "The observed effect is nowhere near the null distribution")
print(p)

cat(sprintf("null distribution: mean %.5f, SD %.5f, range %.4f to %.4f\n",
            mean(r1$null), sd(r1$null), min(r1$null), max(r1$null)))
## null distribution: mean -0.00003, SD 0.00311, range -0.0109 to 0.0117
cat(sprintf("observed statistic %.4f -> %.1f null standard deviations away\n",
            r1$obs, (r1$obs - mean(r1$null)) / sd(r1$null)))
## observed statistic 0.2594 -> 83.5 null standard deviations away
cat(sprintf("permutation p-value (one-sided) = %.5f  <- the smallest 5,000 permutations can report is %.5f\n",
            r1$p, 1 / 5001))
## permutation p-value (one-sided) = 0.00020  <- the smallest 5,000 permutations can report is 0.00020

Figure 1. Null distribution of the difference in mean similarity score between actives and decoys, built by shuffling the active/decoy labels 5,000 times (the x-axis is cut at 0.28 so that both the null cloud and the observed value are visible). Under the null the difference is centred on zero with a standard deviation of 0.0031 and never exceeds 0.012; the observed difference of 0.2594 sits 83.5 null standard deviations to the right. The reported p-value is 1/5001 = 0.0002 — the smallest value this many permutations can produce — and the honest way to write it in a paper is p < 2 × 10−4 (5,000 permutations), not “p = 0”.

Two details of the implementation matter. The +1 in the numerator and denominator is not cosmetic: without it a p-value of exactly zero is possible, which is a probability statement that cannot be true, and the corrected version is the valid Monte-Carlo p-value. And the resolution of a permutation test is bounded by the number of permutations: 5,000 shuffles can never report anything below 2 × 10−4, so if you need a smaller p-value you must either run more permutations or use a parametric approximation.

2.1 A worked example traced by hand

The permutation idea is clearest when the number of permutations is small enough to enumerate completely. Take the six replica means of the C-alpha RMSD from the molecular-dynamics dataset — 300 K: 0.1098, 0.1595, 0.2515 nm; 340 K: 0.1211, 0.1884, 0.1504 nm — and ask whether temperature changed the mean.

Observed difference of means: (0.1098 + 0.1595 + 0.2515)/3 − (0.1211 + 0.1884 + 0.1504)/3 = 0.17360 − 0.15330 = 0.02030 nm.

There are \(\binom{6}{3} = 20\) ways of splitting six numbers into two groups of three. Under the null hypothesis that the temperature label is irrelevant, each of those 20 labellings was equally likely. Here are the first few, sorted by the absolute difference they produce:

rank group “A” mean A mean B |difference|
1 0.2515, 0.1884, 0.1595 0.1998 0.1271 0.0727
2 0.2515, 0.1884, 0.1504 0.1968 0.1301 0.0666
3 0.2515, 0.1884, 0.1211 0.1870 0.1399 0.0471
… … … … …
— 0.1098, 0.1595, 0.2515 (the observed one) 0.1736 0.1533 0.0203

The two-sided p-value is the proportion of the 20 labellings whose absolute difference is at least 0.0203. The next chunk enumerates all twenty.

per_run <- md_obs[, .(mean_rmsd = mean(rmsd_ca_nm)), by = .(condition, replica)]
A <- per_run[condition == "A", mean_rmsd]          ## 300 K replica means (nm)
B <- per_run[condition == "B", mean_rmsd]          ## 340 K replica means (nm)
allv <- c(A, B); obs_d <- mean(A) - mean(B)
cmb  <- combn(6, 3)
enum <- data.table(
  group_A  = apply(cmb, 2, function(k) paste(sprintf("%.4f", allv[k]), collapse = ", ")),
  meanA    = apply(cmb, 2, function(k) mean(allv[k])),
  meanB    = apply(cmb, 2, function(k) mean(allv[-k])))
enum[, abs_diff := abs(meanA - meanB)]
setorder(enum, -abs_diff)
p_exact <- mean(enum$abs_diff >= abs(obs_d) - 1e-12)
cat(sprintf("observed difference %.5f nm\n", obs_d))
## observed difference 0.02030 nm
cat(sprintf("number of possible labellings: %d\n", nrow(enum)))
## number of possible labellings: 20
cat(sprintf("labellings at least as extreme: %d  ->  exact two-sided p = %.3f\n",
            sum(enum$abs_diff >= abs(obs_d) - 1e-12), p_exact))
## labellings at least as extreme: 16  ->  exact two-sided p = 0.800
cat(sprintf("smallest two-sided p attainable with 3 vs 3 replicas: 2/20 = %.2f\n", 2 / 20))
## smallest two-sided p attainable with 3 vs 3 replicas: 2/20 = 0.10
print(head(enum[, .(group_A, meanA, meanB, abs_diff)], 4))
##                   group_A     meanA     meanB   abs_diff
##                    <char>     <num>     <num>      <num>
## 1: 0.1098, 0.1211, 0.1504 0.1270809 0.1998157 0.07273481
## 2: 0.1595, 0.2515, 0.1884 0.1998157 0.1270809 0.07273481
## 3: 0.1098, 0.1595, 0.1211 0.1301423 0.1967544 0.06661216
## 4: 0.2515, 0.1884, 0.1504 0.1967544 0.1301423 0.06661216
cat("rank of the observed labelling:",
    which(abs(enum$abs_diff - abs(obs_d)) < 1e-12)[1], "of 20\n")
## rank of the observed labelling: 15 of 20

The hand calculation and the code agree: the top of the enumeration is 0.0727, 0.0727, 0.0666, 0.0666 — every split and its mirror image give the same absolute difference, so the values come in pairs — the observed split ranks 15th of 20, and the exact two-sided p-value is 0.800. More importantly, the printed line about resolution is a fact about the design, not about the data: with three replicas per condition there are only 20 labellings, so the smallest two-sided p-value the experiment can possibly produce is 2/20 = 0.10. A 3-versus-3 permutation test can never be significant at the 0.05 level, whatever the data look like. No amount of computation fixes that; only more replicas do, which is the subject of §8.

3. The classical tests are special cases

Before computers, enumerating permutations was impossible, so the field derived formulas that approximate the permutation null under extra assumptions. Each classical test is a shortcut of this kind, and knowing which assumption buys which shortcut is how you choose one.

test compares R function key assumptions
Student’s t two means t.test(var.equal = TRUE) normal data, equal variances, independence
Welch’s t two means t.test() (the default) normal data, unequal variances allowed[4]
paired t mean of within-pair differences t.test(paired = TRUE) normal differences, independent pairs
Mann–Whitney U stochastic ordering wilcox.test(x, y) independent, continuous-ish data[5]
Wilcoxon signed-rank within-pair differences wilcox.test(d) symmetric differences[6]
one-way ANOVA k means aov() / anova(lm()) normal, equal variances, independence
Kruskal–Wallis k distributions by rank kruskal.test() independence[7]
chi-square counts in a contingency table chisq.test() expected counts ≳ 5[8]
Fisher’s exact counts in a 2 × 2 table fisher.test() fixed margins
permutation anything written by hand exchangeability under the null

The first comparison checks the claim directly: on the actives-versus-decoys data, do the shortcut and the permutation test agree?

r1m <- permutation_test(act, dec, stat = function(x, y) median(x) - median(y), n_perm = 5000, seed = 1)
t_eq <- t.test(act, dec, var.equal = TRUE, alternative = "greater")
t_we <- t.test(act, dec, alternative = "greater")
u    <- suppressWarnings(wilcox.test(act, dec, alternative = "greater"))
comp <- data.table(
  test = c("Student t (equal var)", "Welch t", "Mann-Whitney U",
           "permutation (means, 5000)", "permutation (medians, 5000)"),
  statistic = c(t_eq$statistic, t_we$statistic, u$statistic, r1$obs, r1m$obs),
  p = c(pfmt(t_eq$p.value), pfmt(t_we$p.value), pfmt(u$p.value),
        sprintf("%.5f", r1$p), sprintf("%.5f", r1m$p)))
grp <- factor(rep(c("active", "decoy"), c(length(act), length(dec))))
lev <- leveneTest(c(act, dec) ~ grp)
cat(sprintf("variance ratio actives/decoys: %.2f  (Levene F = %.0f, p = %s)\n",
            var(act) / var(dec), lev[1, 2], pfmt(lev[1, 3])))
## variance ratio actives/decoys: 24.44  (Levene F = 9487, p = < 1e-300)
cat(sprintf("group sizes: %d vs %d | Welch df = %.0f\n", length(act), length(dec), t_we$parameter))
## group sizes: 1302 vs 10691 | Welch df = 1314
knitr::kable(comp, digits = 4)
test statistic p
Student t (equal var) 1.370101e+02 < 1e-300
Welch t 5.511510e+01 < 1e-300
Mann-Whitney U 1.323921e+07 < 1e-300
permutation (means, 5000) 2.594000e-01 0.00020
permutation (medians, 5000) 2.668000e-01 0.00020

All five routes agree that the score separates actives from decoys. The agreement is the point: when the assumptions hold well enough, the parametric shortcut reproduces the permutation answer at a fraction of the cost. Two R-specific observations. First, the two t-statistics differ enormously — 137.0 for Student against 55.1 for Welch — because the variance ratio between the groups is 24.4 and Levene’s test rejects equality decisively; with 1,302 actives against 10,691 decoys the pooled variance of the Student version is dominated by the tight decoy group, which inflates the statistic. Welch’s test is the default in R for exactly this reason[4], and you have to ask for the wrong test explicitly. Second, both parametric p-values underflow to zero in double precision, which is why they print as “< 1e-300” rather than as a number.

What none of the five numbers tells us is whether the score is useful. They all answer “is the difference exactly zero?”, a question whose answer was known in advance. Section 5 replaces them with a number that answers the real question.

3.1 Paired data: the single most valuable design feature

When each measurement in one group has a natural partner in the other — the same patient, the same compound in two assays, the same system before and after a mutation — the paired test removes between-subject variation by analysing the within-pair differences. The gain is usually larger than anything else available to the experimenter.

gmeta <- meta[, .(sample_id, patient_id, status)]
dis <- gmeta[status == "diseased"][order(patient_id)]
hea <- gmeta[status == "healthy"][order(patient_id)]
stopifnot(identical(dis$patient_id, hea$patient_id))      ## same patient order in both vectors
gene  <- "PLA2R1"
rowg  <- expr[symbol == gene]
d_vals <- as.numeric(rowg[, dis$sample_id, with = FALSE])
h_vals <- as.numeric(rowg[, hea$sample_id, with = FALSE])
dvec   <- d_vals - h_vals
op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2.4, 1), cex = 0.75)
plot(NA, xlim = c(0.8, 2.2), ylim = range(c(d_vals, h_vals)), xaxt = "n",
     xlab = "", ylab = sprintf("log2 expression of %s", gene), main = "each line is one patient")
axis(1, at = c(1, 2), labels = c("healthy site", "diseased site"))
segments(1, h_vals, 2, d_vals, col = "#99999999")
points(rep(1, length(h_vals)), h_vals, pch = 19, cex = 0.5, col = PAL["green"])
points(rep(2, length(d_vals)), d_vals, pch = 19, cex = 0.5, col = PAL["orange"])
hist(dvec, breaks = 22, col = PAL["blue"], border = NA, main = "the paired test works on this histogram",
     xlab = "within-patient difference (diseased - healthy)", ylab = "patients")
abline(v = 0, lty = 2, lwd = 1.5)

par(op)
set.seed(11)
flips <- replicate(5000, mean(sample(c(-1, 1), length(dvec), replace = TRUE) * dvec))
cat(sprintf("unpaired Welch t : t = %6.3f, p = %s\n", t.test(d_vals, h_vals)$statistic,
            pfmt(t.test(d_vals, h_vals)$p.value)))
## unpaired Welch t : t = -9.646, p = 6.07e-17
cat(sprintf("paired t         : t = %6.3f, p = %s\n", t.test(d_vals, h_vals, paired = TRUE)$statistic,
            pfmt(t.test(d_vals, h_vals, paired = TRUE)$p.value)))
## paired t         : t = -13.305, p = 1.33e-20
cat(sprintf("Wilcoxon signed  : V = %6.0f, p = %s\n", wilcox.test(dvec)$statistic,
            pfmt(wilcox.test(dvec)$p.value)))
## Wilcoxon signed  : V =     55, p = 5.67e-12
cat(sprintf("sign-flip permutation p = %.4f\n", (1 + sum(abs(flips) >= abs(mean(dvec)))) / 5001))
## sign-flip permutation p = 0.0002
cat(sprintf("mean within-patient difference %.3f log2 units\n", mean(dvec)))
## mean within-patient difference -0.980 log2 units
cat(sprintf("between-patient SD %.3f | within-pair SD %.3f -> pairing removes %.0f%% of the noise\n",
            sd(c(d_vals, h_vals)), sd(dvec), 100 * (1 - sd(dvec) / sd(c(d_vals, h_vals)))))
## between-patient SD 0.772 | within-pair SD 0.612 -> pairing removes 21% of the noise

Figure 2. Expression of PLA2R1 in 69 matched pairs of gingival tissue. Left: each grey line joins the healthy and diseased sample of one patient; the lines are mostly parallel and mostly descending, which is exactly the situation the paired test exploits — patients differ widely in overall level, but within a patient the direction is consistent. Right: the histogram of the 69 within-patient differences is shifted clearly below zero, with a mean of −0.980 log2 units (a two-fold reduction). The printed statistics show the consequence: on identical numbers the paired p-value is 1.3 × 10−20 against 6.1 × 10−17 unpaired, because working within patients removes 21 % of the standard deviation — and that modest-sounding reduction is amplified by the √n in the test statistic.

The correct permutation null for a paired design is not a shuffle of the group labels but a random flip of the sign of each within-pair difference, because under the null the diseased and healthy label within a patient are exchangeable. The sign-flip p-value hits its resolution floor of 1/5001 = 0.0002, consistent with the Wilcoxon and paired-t results. Choosing the wrong exchangeability structure is the most common way to get a permutation test wrong.

3.2 More than two groups, and counts

cnt  <- sort(table(exact$scaffold_smiles), decreasing = TRUE)
top5 <- names(cnt)[1:5]
ser  <- rbindlist(lapply(seq_along(top5), function(i)
  data.table(series = sprintf("S%d", i), pActivity = exact[scaffold_smiles == top5[i], pActivity])))
ser[, series := factor(series, levels = sprintf("S%d", 1:5))]
set.seed(12)
p <- ggplot(ser, aes(series, pActivity)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA, fill = "grey92") +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.16, size = 0.5, alpha = 0.4, colour = PAL["blue"]) +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "point", shape = 23, size = 1.8, fill = PAL["orange"]) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "pActivity",
       title = "Five Bemis-Murcko scaffold series of the ROCK1 dataset")
print(p)

fit_aov <- summary(aov(pActivity ~ series, ser))[[1]]
kw <- kruskal.test(pActivity ~ series, ser)
cat(sprintf("one-way ANOVA   : F = %.2f, p = %s\n", fit_aov[1, 4], pfmt(fit_aov[1, 5])))
## one-way ANOVA   : F = 31.87, p = 7.23e-23
cat(sprintf("Kruskal-Wallis  : H = %.2f, p = %s\n", kw$statistic, pfmt(kw$p.value)))
## Kruskal-Wallis  : H = 84.08, p = 2.38e-17
cat(sprintf("Levene equal-variance test p = %.5f\n", leveneTest(pActivity ~ series, ser)[1, 3]))
## Levene equal-variance test p = 0.00001
print(ser[, .(n = .N, mean = mean(pActivity), sd = sd(pActivity), median = median(pActivity),
              shapiro_p = shapiro.test(pActivity)$p.value), by = series])
##    series     n     mean        sd median   shapiro_p
##    <fctr> <int>    <num>     <num>  <num>       <num>
## 1:     S1   207 7.396700 0.8121831 7.5210 0.005117237
## 2:     S2    59 6.069373 1.0034919 6.2270 0.075727148
## 3:     S3    43 6.978279 0.9543079 7.0220 0.845159180
## 4:     S4    38 6.832105 0.4761410 6.8655 0.310257137
## 5:     S5    33 7.338091 0.6142739 7.4270 0.148484257

Figure 3. Potency distributions of the five largest scaffold series (diamonds: group means). The series differ by more than a log unit in median potency, with visibly different spreads and sample sizes (207, 59, 43, 38 and 33 compounds). Both the ANOVA (F = 31.87) and the Kruskal–Wallis test (H = 84.08) reject the hypothesis that all five series have the same central potency, with p-values of 7 × 10−23 and 2 × 10−17, and they agree despite the ANOVA’s equal-variance assumption being violated (Levene p below 10−4) — a reminder that these tests are fairly robust when sample sizes are large, and that the consequence of a violation should be checked rather than assumed fatal. Note also that Shapiro–Wilk rejects normality for the largest series (p = 0.005) and accepts it for the four small ones, which is the sample-size artefact of Unit 7 §5, not evidence that the large series is the problematic one.

An omnibus test tells you only that the groups are not all the same. It does not say which pair differs, and running all ten pairwise comparisons afterwards reintroduces exactly the multiplicity problem of §6. The disciplined sequence is: pre-specify the contrast of interest; if there is no such contrast, run the omnibus test first and correct the follow-ups.

For categorical data the same logic applies to a contingency table. The chi-square test compares observed counts with the counts expected if the two classifications were independent; Fisher’s exact test computes the same probability exactly from the hypergeometric distribution, which is what you need when any expected count is small.

cut_off  <- quantile(s, 0.90)                       ## call the top 10 % of the library a 'hit'
dec_rows <- lib[keep][y == 0]
tbl <- table(decoy_set = dec_rows$decoy_set, flagged = s[y == 0] >= cut_off)
ch  <- chisq.test(tbl); fi <- fisher.test(tbl)
cat(sprintf("score cut-off (90th percentile of the library): %.3f\n", cut_off))
## score cut-off (90th percentile of the library): 0.267
print(tbl)
##                   flagged
## decoy_set          FALSE TRUE
##   property_matched  6784  139
##   random            3747   21
cat("\nexpected counts under independence:\n"); print(round(ch$expected, 1))
## 
## expected counts under independence:
##                   flagged
## decoy_set           FALSE  TRUE
##   property_matched 6819.4 103.6
##   random           3711.6  56.4
cat(sprintf("\nchi-square = %.2f, df = %d, p = %s\n", ch$statistic, ch$parameter, pfmt(ch$p.value)))
## 
## chi-square = 33.85, df = 1, p = 5.97e-09
cat(sprintf("Fisher exact odds ratio (as the table is given) = %.3f, p = %s\n",
            fi$estimate, pfmt(fi$p.value)))
## Fisher exact odds ratio (as the table is given) = 0.274, p = 2.99e-10
cat(sprintf("false-positive rate: property-matched %.2f%% | random %.2f%%\n",
            100 * tbl[1, 2] / sum(tbl[1, ]), 100 * tbl[2, 2] / sum(tbl[2, ])))
## false-positive rate: property-matched 2.01% | random 0.56%

The two tests agree closely, as they must when every expected count is comfortably above five (the smallest expected count here is 56.4); the exact test matters when a cell contains a handful of observations, which is the common situation in a small clinical table. Note the orientation trap: fisher.test returns 0.274 because it takes the table as given — rows ordered property_matched, random and columns FALSE, TRUE — and the quantity we want, the odds of being flagged for a matched decoy relative to a random one, is its reciprocal, 3.66. Always state which way round an odds ratio is defined. The odds ratio is the effect size for a 2 × 2 table, and it is the number that belongs in the text — “property-matched decoys were flagged three and a half times as often as random ones” is informative in a way that “χ² = 33.9, p = 6 × 10−9” is not.

4. What a p-value is, and the four things it is not

A p-value is the probability of data at least as extreme as the observed data, computed under the assumption that the null hypothesis and the whole statistical model are true[9][10]. From that definition, four common readings are wrong:

  • It is not the probability that the null hypothesis is true. That quantity requires a prior and is computed in Unit 10.
  • It is not the probability that the result will replicate. A study with p = 0.05 has roughly even odds of reaching p < 0.05 again[11].
  • It is not a measure of effect size. With 12,000 molecules a difference of 0.001 in mean score reaches p below 10−10; with three replicas a difference of 0.1 nm cannot reach 0.05 at all.
  • It is not a decision. The 0.05 threshold is a convention, not a property of nature, and dichotomising a continuous measure of evidence at it is the practice a large part of the statistical community now argues against[12][13].

The constructive statement is the relationship between the test and the interval: a two-sided test at level α rejects exactly when the (1 − α) confidence interval for the effect excludes the null value. The interval therefore contains the p-value’s information plus the effect size plus the precision, which is why reporting the interval instead of the p-value loses nothing and gains everything.

set.seed(13)
pci <- rbindlist(lapply(c(10, 25, 60, 150, 400), function(n) {
  sa <- sample(act, n); sd_ <- sample(dec, n)
  tt <- t.test(sa, sd_)
  data.table(n_per_group = n, difference = mean(sa) - mean(sd_),
             ci_low = tt$conf.int[1], ci_high = tt$conf.int[2], p = tt$p.value,
             ci_excludes_0 = !(tt$conf.int[1] <= 0 & 0 <= tt$conf.int[2]),
             p_below_0.05 = tt$p.value < 0.05)
}))
p <- ggplot(pci, aes(difference, factor(n_per_group))) +
  geom_errorbarh(aes(xmin = ci_low, xmax = ci_high), height = 0.2, colour = PAL["blue"]) +
  geom_point(colour = PAL["blue"], size = 1.8) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = PAL["orange"], linetype = 2) +
  geom_text(aes(x = ci_high, label = sprintf("p = %.2g", p)), hjust = -0.1, size = 2.6) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(-0.02, 0.42)) +
  labs(x = "difference in mean similarity score (actives - decoys), 95 % CI",
       y = "compounds per group", title = "Every p-value is a confidence interval seen through a keyhole")
print(p)

knitr::kable(pci, digits = 4)
n_per_group difference ci_low ci_high p ci_excludes_0 p_below_0.05
10 0.2144 0.0894 0.3395 0.0036 TRUE TRUE
25 0.2659 0.2122 0.3196 0.0000 TRUE TRUE
60 0.2453 0.1999 0.2907 0.0000 TRUE TRUE
150 0.2834 0.2540 0.3127 0.0000 TRUE TRUE
400 0.2567 0.2400 0.2733 0.0000 TRUE TRUE

Figure 4. The same comparison at five sample sizes. The point estimate hardly changes — it ranges from 0.214 to 0.283, because the effect is what it is — while the interval narrows as √n, from a width of 0.25 at n = 10 to 0.033 at n = 400, and the p-value falls from 3.6 × 10−3 to 6 × 10−109. In every row the verdict “p < 0.05” coincides exactly with “the interval excludes zero”, as the last two columns of the table confirm. The interval additionally shows that at n = 10 the data are compatible with differences between 0.089 and 0.339, information that no p-value carries.

5. Effect sizes, and their intervals

An effect size is a number that answers “how big?” in units that transfer between studies[14]. The ones we need:

  • Cohen’s d = (mean₁ − mean₂)/spooled, the difference in pooled standard deviations.
  • Hedges’ g = d × (1 − 3/(4(n₁+n₂) − 9)), a small-sample bias correction[15].
  • Cliff’s delta = P(X > Y) − P(X < Y), a non-parametric dominance measure in [−1, 1][16].
  • Rank-biserial correlation = 2U/(n₁n₂) − 1, the same quantity derived from the Mann–Whitney statistic.
  • Odds ratio for 2 × 2 tables.

In R these live in the effectsize package[35], which returns each one with a confidence interval by default — analytic for d and g, and from the rank statistic for the dominance measures.

5.1 Cohen’s d traced by hand

Take the first five pActivity values of each of the two largest scaffold series: series 1 gives 7.52, 8.10, 7.00, 6.70 and 7.40; series 2 gives 5.70, 6.23, 7.00, 5.52 and 6.10 (the code below uses the real full series; these excerpts are for the hand calculation).

Mean₁ = (7.52 + 8.10 + 7.00 + 6.70 + 7.40)/5 = 36.72/5 = 7.344. Mean₂ = (5.70 + 6.23 + 7.00 + 5.52 + 6.10)/5 = 30.55/5 = 6.110.

Deviations from mean₁: 0.176, 0.756, −0.344, −0.644, 0.056 → squares 0.0310 + 0.5715 + 0.1183 + 0.4147 + 0.0031 = 1.1386, so s₁² = 1.1386/4 = 0.2847. Deviations from mean₂: −0.410, 0.120, 0.890, −0.590, −0.010 → squares 0.1681 + 0.0144 + 0.7921 + 0.3481 + 0.0001 = 1.3228, so s₂² = 1.3228/4 = 0.3307.

Pooled variance = ((5−1)·0.2847 + (5−1)·0.3307)/(5 + 5 − 2) = (1.1386 + 1.3228)/8 = 0.3077, so spooled = 0.5547.

d = (7.344 − 6.110)/0.5547 = 2.225 — a very large effect by any convention (0.2 small, 0.5 medium, 0.8 large). The next chunk reproduces this and then computes every effect size, with its interval, on the full series.

h1 <- c(7.52, 8.10, 7.00, 6.70, 7.40); h2 <- c(5.70, 6.23, 7.00, 5.52, 6.10)
sp <- sqrt(((length(h1) - 1) * var(h1) + (length(h2) - 1) * var(h2)) / (length(h1) + length(h2) - 2))
cat(sprintf("hand check: mean1 %.3f, mean2 %.3f, s_pooled %.4f, Cohen d = %.3f\n",
            mean(h1), mean(h2), sp, (mean(h1) - mean(h2)) / sp))
## hand check: mean1 7.344, mean2 6.110, s_pooled 0.5547, Cohen d = 2.225
s1 <- exact[scaffold_smiles == names(cnt)[1], pActivity]
s2 <- exact[scaffold_smiles == names(cnt)[2], pActivity]
es <- rbindlist(list(
  cbind(data.table(effect_size = "Cohen d"),        as.data.table(cohens_d(s1, s2))[, .(estimate = Cohens_d, CI_low, CI_high)]),
  cbind(data.table(effect_size = "Hedges g"),       as.data.table(hedges_g(s1, s2))[, .(estimate = Hedges_g, CI_low, CI_high)]),
  cbind(data.table(effect_size = "Cliff delta"),    as.data.table(cliffs_delta(s1, s2))[, .(estimate = r_rank_biserial, CI_low, CI_high)]),
  cbind(data.table(effect_size = "rank-biserial r"), as.data.table(rank_biserial(s1, s2))[, .(estimate = r_rank_biserial, CI_low, CI_high)])))
p <- ggplot(es, aes(estimate, factor(effect_size, levels = rev(effect_size)))) +
  geom_errorbarh(aes(xmin = CI_low, xmax = CI_high), height = 0.2, colour = PAL["blue"]) +
  geom_point(colour = PAL["blue"], size = 1.9) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = PAL["orange"], linetype = 2) +
  labs(x = "effect size, series 1 vs series 2 (95 % CI)", y = NULL,
       title = "Four effect sizes for one comparison")
print(p)

cat(sprintf("series 1: n = %d, mean %.3f | series 2: n = %d, mean %.3f | difference %.3f log units\n",
            length(s1), mean(s1), length(s2), mean(s2), mean(s1) - mean(s2)))
## series 1: n = 207, mean 7.397 | series 2: n = 59, mean 6.069 | difference 1.327 log units
cat(sprintf("P(a random series-1 compound is more potent than a random series-2 compound) = %.3f\n",
            mean(outer(s1, s2, ">"))))
## P(a random series-1 compound is more potent than a random series-2 compound) = 0.847
knitr::kable(es, digits = 3)
effect_size estimate CI_low CI_high
Cohen d 1.547 1.228 1.864
Hedges g 1.543 1.225 1.859
Cliff delta 0.694 0.596 0.771
rank-biserial r 0.694 0.596 0.771

Figure 5. Four effect sizes for the same comparison between the two largest scaffold series, with 95 % intervals. Cohen’s d (1.547) and Hedges’ g (1.543) are nearly identical because the samples are large — the correction factor is 0.3 % — and both say the two series differ by about one and a half pooled standard deviations. Cliff’s delta and the rank-biserial correlation are exactly the same number here (0.694, interval 0.596 to 0.771) because effectsize implements Cliff’s delta as the rank-biserial correlation, of which it is an algebraic rearrangement; the direct computation below the figure confirms the interpretation: a randomly chosen series-1 compound is more potent than a randomly chosen series-2 compound 84.7 % of the time. None of the intervals comes close to zero.

For a 2 × 2 table the matching effect size is the odds ratio, and its interval is computed on the log scale, where the standard error is the square root of the sum of the reciprocals of the four cells.

a_ <- tbl[1, 2]; b_ <- tbl[1, 1]      ## property-matched: flagged, not flagged
c_ <- tbl[2, 2]; d_ <- tbl[2, 1]      ## random decoys:    flagged, not flagged
or_hat <- (a_ * d_) / (b_ * c_)
se_log <- sqrt(1 / a_ + 1 / b_ + 1 / c_ + 1 / d_)
ci <- exp(log(or_hat) + c(-1.96, 1.96) * se_log)
cat(sprintf("property-matched decoys flagged: %d / %d (%.2f %%)\n", a_, a_ + b_, 100 * a_ / (a_ + b_)))
## property-matched decoys flagged: 139 / 6923 (2.01 %)
cat(sprintf("random decoys flagged          : %d / %d (%.2f %%)\n", c_, c_ + d_, 100 * c_ / (c_ + d_)))
## random decoys flagged          : 21 / 3768 (0.56 %)
cat(sprintf("odds ratio %.2f, 95%% CI [%.2f, %.2f]  (log-scale SE %.3f)\n", or_hat, ci[1], ci[2], se_log))
## odds ratio 3.66, 95% CI [2.31, 5.79]  (log-scale SE 0.235)
cat(sprintf("risk ratio %.2f  <- the easier quantity to explain in a paper\n",
            (a_ / (a_ + b_)) / (c_ / (c_ + d_))))
## risk ratio 3.60  <- the easier quantity to explain in a paper
cat(sprintf("Fisher exact p = %s | fisher.test's own CI on its orientation: [%.3f, %.3f]\n",
            pfmt(fi$p.value), fi$conf.int[1], fi$conf.int[2]))
## Fisher exact p = 2.99e-10 | fisher.test's own CI on its orientation: [0.164, 0.436]

The interval excludes 1 comfortably, so the enrichment of property-matched decoys among the false hits is not a fluctuation: a similarity score given decoys chosen to resemble the actives physically produces 2.01 % false positives against 0.56 % for random decoys — an odds ratio of 3.66 (95 % CI 2.31 to 5.79) and a risk ratio of 3.60. That is a statement about the benchmark, not about the method, and it is why Unit 19 insists that an enrichment number is meaningless without the decoy-design description. Note that fisher.test reports the interval for the reciprocal orientation, which is the same statement upside down.

The practical advice is to report one effect size, chosen to match the test, with its interval: d or g alongside a t-test, Cliff’s delta or the rank-biserial correlation alongside a rank test, an odds ratio alongside a contingency table. Then translate it into the units of the field — “1.33 log units, i.e. a twenty-fold difference in potency” — because that is the sentence a chemist or a clinician can act on.

Exercise 1

Compute Cohen’s d and the rank-biserial correlation for the comparison of MolWt between the actives and the property-matched decoys of the screening library, and then between the actives and the random decoys (lib[label == 1, MolWt] versus lib[decoy_set == “property_matched”, MolWt]). Which decoy set is better matched, and how does the effect size you obtain change the interpretation of a screening benchmark run against each? (Unit 19 develops this into the artificial-enrichment diagnostic.)

6. Multiple comparisons

Run one test at α = 0.05 on data with no effect and you have a 5 % chance of a false positive. Run 1,000 such tests and you expect 50 of them. Any experiment that measures many things at once — a transcriptome, a descriptor panel, a docking campaign over many targets — is in this regime by construction, and the correction is not optional.

Two different guarantees are on offer, and confusing them is the usual mistake:

  • Family-wise error rate (FWER) — the probability of at least one false positive among all tests. Controlled by Bonferroni (reject when p ≤ α/m) and, more powerfully and with the same guarantee, by Holm’s step-down procedure[17]. Appropriate when a single false claim is costly: one confirmatory endpoint, one go/no-go decision.
  • False discovery rate (FDR) — the expected proportion of false positives among the tests you call significant. Controlled by Benjamini–Hochberg (BH)[18]. Appropriate for screening: a gene list or a hit list is a set of leads, and tolerating 5 % wrong leads to find many more true ones is a sensible trade.

All three are p.adjust(p, method = ...) in base R — "bonferroni", "holm", "BH" — which returns adjusted p-values rather than a reject/accept vector, so the comparison with α happens afterwards. The BH procedure itself is three lines: sort the m p-values ascending, find the largest rank k with \(p_{(k)} \le \frac{k}{m}\alpha\), and reject all hypotheses up to that rank. The corresponding adjusted p-value (q-value in the loose sense) is the running minimum of \(\frac{m}{k}p_{(k)}\) from the largest rank downwards. Storey’s refinement additionally estimates the proportion \(\pi_0\) of true nulls and gains power when it is well below 1[19].

set.seed(0)
sel <- sort(sample(nrow(expr), 1000))
Xd  <- as.matrix(expr[sel, dis$sample_id, with = FALSE])    ## 1000 genes x 69 diseased samples
Xh  <- as.matrix(expr[sel, hea$sample_id, with = FALSE])    ## the matching healthy samples
Dm  <- Xd - Xh; npair <- ncol(Dm)
t_paired <- rowMeans(Dm) / (apply(Dm, 1, sd) / sqrt(npair))
p_paired <- 2 * pt(-abs(t_paired), df = npair - 1)
v1 <- apply(Xd, 1, var); v2 <- apply(Xh, 1, var)
se_u <- sqrt(v1 / npair + v2 / npair)
df_u <- (v1 / npair + v2 / npair)^2 /
        ((v1 / npair)^2 / (npair - 1) + (v2 / npair)^2 / (npair - 1))
p_unpaired <- 2 * pt(-abs((rowMeans(Xd) - rowMeans(Xh)) / se_u), df = df_u)
stopifnot(abs(p_paired[1] - t.test(Xd[1, ], Xh[1, ], paired = TRUE)$p.value) < 1e-12)
log2fc <- rowMeans(Dm)
summary_dt <- rbindlist(lapply(list(`paired t` = p_paired, `unpaired Welch t` = p_unpaired), function(p)
  data.table(raw = sum(p < 0.05), Bonferroni = sum(p.adjust(p, "bonferroni") < 0.05),
             Holm = sum(p.adjust(p, "holm") < 0.05), BH = sum(p.adjust(p, "BH") < 0.05))), idcol = "design")
hist_dt <- rbind(data.table(p = p_paired, design = "paired t"),
                 data.table(p = p_unpaired, design = "unpaired Welch t"))
p <- ggplot(hist_dt, aes(p)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 40, fill = PAL["blue"], colour = NA) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1000 / 40, colour = PAL["orange"], linetype = 2) +
  facet_wrap(~ design) +
  labs(x = "p-value", y = "genes", title = "p-value histograms: a spike at zero on a flat background")
print(p)

cat(sprintf("genes tested: %d | mean |log2 fold change| = %.3f | genes with |log2FC| > 1: %d\n",
            length(p_paired), mean(abs(log2fc)), sum(abs(log2fc) > 1)))
## genes tested: 1000 | mean |log2 fold change| = 0.395 | genes with |log2FC| > 1: 46
knitr::kable(summary_dt)
design raw Bonferroni Holm BH
paired t 756 534 551 747
unpaired Welch t 701 453 470 682

Figure 6. Histograms of the 1,000 p-values under the two designs; the dashed line is the height a uniform histogram would have if every null were true. Neither is uniform: both show the enormous spike near zero characteristic of a real, pervasive biological signal — periodontitis changes the expression of a large fraction of the transcriptome in affected tissue. The paired design (left) pushes more mass into the first bin than the unpaired one (right). The table gives the counts: of 1,000 genes, 756 reach raw p < 0.05 under pairing against 701 unpaired, and after Benjamini–Hochberg correction 747 versus 682 survive. The family-wise procedures are far stricter: under pairing they keep 534 (Bonferroni) and 551 (Holm), and without pairing 453 and 470 — Holm rejecting slightly more than Bonferroni in both designs, as it must.

Three readings follow. First, the design matters more than the correction: pairing recovers 65 more genes after BH than the unpaired analysis does, and no choice of adjustment method can make up for the lost information. Second, BH costs almost nothing here and Bonferroni costs a lot — when the signal is pervasive, controlling the probability of a single error discards more than two hundred true findings. Third, these counts are so high only because the biological effect is strong; in a typical study the first bin is a modest excess over a uniform background, and then the choice of procedure decides whether the paper has ten hits or none.

The p-value histogram is a diagnostic, not decoration

Always plot it before correcting. A uniform histogram means no signal. A spike at zero on a flat background is the healthy pattern. A histogram that rises towards 1, or is bumpy in the middle, means the tests are misspecified — wrong null, dependence between tests, or discrete data — and no multiplicity correction repairs a wrong null. 

bh_by_hand <- function(p, alpha = 0.05) {
  m <- length(p); o <- order(p); ps <- p[o]
  below <- which(ps <= alpha * seq_len(m) / m)
  k <- if (length(below)) max(below) else 0
  q <- rev(cummin(rev(m / seq_len(m) * ps)))        ## running minimum from the largest rank down
  qv <- numeric(m); qv[o] <- pmin(q, 1)
  list(k = k, q = qv)
}
bh <- bh_by_hand(p_paired, 0.05)
cat(sprintf("BH by hand rejects %d | p.adjust rejects %d | identical adjusted p-values: %s\n",
            bh$k, sum(p.adjust(p_paired, "BH") < 0.05),
            isTRUE(all.equal(bh$q, p.adjust(p_paired, "BH")))))
## BH by hand rejects 747 | p.adjust rejects 747 | identical adjusted p-values: TRUE
cat(sprintf("BH cut-off: the %dth smallest p-value, p = %.3e (Bonferroni cut-off would be %.3e)\n",
            bh$k, sort(p_paired)[bh$k], 0.05 / length(p_paired)))
## BH cut-off: the 747th smallest p-value, p = 3.620e-02 (Bonferroni cut-off would be 5.000e-05)
pi0 <- min(1, 2 * mean(p_paired > 0.5))
cat(sprintf("Storey pi0 estimate (fraction of true nulls): %.3f -> BH is conservative by a factor %.1f here\n",
            pi0, 1 / pi0))
## Storey pi0 estimate (fraction of true nulls): 0.124 -> BH is conservative by a factor 8.1 here
srt <- sort(p_paired); m <- length(srt)
p <- ggplot(data.frame(rank = seq_len(m), p = srt), aes(rank, p)) +
  geom_point(size = 0.4, colour = PAL["blue"]) +
  geom_line(data = data.frame(rank = seq_len(m), p = 0.05 * seq_len(m) / m), colour = PAL["orange"]) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.05 / m, linetype = 3) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = bh$k, colour = PAL["green"], linetype = 2) +
  scale_x_log10() + scale_y_log10() +
  labs(x = "rank k", y = "p-value",
       title = sprintf("The Benjamini-Hochberg staircase (rejects the first %d)", bh$k))
print(p)

Figure 7. The BH procedure drawn on log–log axes. The blue points are the 1,000 sorted p-values; the orange line is the BH threshold k·α/m; the procedure rejects everything up to the last crossing, marked by the green dashed line at rank 747, which corresponds to a p-value cut-off of 0.036 — seven hundred times more permissive than the Bonferroni cut-off of 5 × 10−5 (dotted line). The printed Storey estimate of the proportion of true nulls is 0.124, so BH is conservative by a factor of eight on these data: the adaptive version would reject slightly more.

The hand implementation and p.adjust return identical adjusted p-values, which is worth checking once in your life so that the function stops being a black box. Report the adjusted values in the supplementary table, state the method and the α in the methods section, and say how many tests were in the family — a BH correction over 1,000 genes means nothing if the reader does not know whether you tested 1,000 or 20,000.

6.1 A negative control: what the procedure does when nothing is there

The only convincing demonstration that a multiplicity correction works is to run it where the truth is known. We take only the 69 healthy samples, split them at random into two groups, and test all 1,000 genes — there is no disease effect to find, because every sample is healthy.

H <- as.matrix(expr[sel, hea$sample_id, with = FALSE])
set.seed(7)
pm <- sample(ncol(H)); g1 <- pm[1:34]; g2 <- pm[35:69]
v1 <- apply(H[, g1], 1, var); v2 <- apply(H[, g2], 1, var)
se_n <- sqrt(v1 / 34 + v2 / 35)
df_n <- (v1 / 34 + v2 / 35)^2 / ((v1 / 34)^2 / 33 + (v2 / 35)^2 / 34)
p_null <- 2 * pt(-abs((rowMeans(H[, g1]) - rowMeans(H[, g2])) / se_n), df = df_n)
cmp <- rbind(data.table(p = p_null,   what = "healthy vs healthy: flat"),
             data.table(p = p_paired, what = "diseased vs healthy: spike at zero"))
p <- ggplot(cmp, aes(p)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 40, fill = "grey70", colour = NA) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1000 / 40, colour = PAL["orange"], linetype = 2) +
  facet_wrap(~ what, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = "p-value", y = "genes", title = "A null comparison validates the whole pipeline")
print(p)

cat("NULL comparison (69 healthy samples split 34 / 35):\n")
## NULL comparison (69 healthy samples split 34 / 35):
cat(sprintf("  raw p < 0.05        : %3d genes   (expected by chance: ~50)\n", sum(p_null < 0.05)))
##   raw p < 0.05        :   8 genes   (expected by chance: ~50)
cat(sprintf("  Bonferroni          : %3d genes\n", sum(p.adjust(p_null, "bonferroni") < 0.05)))
##   Bonferroni          :   0 genes
cat(sprintf("  Benjamini-Hochberg  : %3d genes\n", sum(p.adjust(p_null, "BH") < 0.05)))
##   Benjamini-Hochberg  :   0 genes
cat(sprintf("  smallest p-value    : %.4f\n", min(p_null)))
##   smallest p-value    : 0.0089
cat("REAL comparison (paired, diseased vs healthy):\n")
## REAL comparison (paired, diseased vs healthy):
cat(sprintf("  raw p < 0.05        : %3d genes\n", sum(p_paired < 0.05)))
##   raw p < 0.05        : 756 genes
cat(sprintf("  Benjamini-Hochberg  : %3d genes\n", sum(p.adjust(p_paired, "BH") < 0.05)))
##   Benjamini-Hochberg  : 747 genes

Figure 8. The same 1,000 genes under a null comparison (left, healthy against healthy) and the real one (right); note the free y-axis. The null histogram is flat, as a correct test on true nulls must be, and the 8 genes that reach raw p < 0.05 — fewer than the ~50 expected, because this split is itself one realisation — are precisely the false positives multiplicity creates. Not one of them survives Benjamini–Hochberg or Bonferroni, and the smallest p-value in the whole family is 0.0089. The real comparison (right) is a different object entirely.

This negative control costs three lines and should be run in every high-dimensional analysis in a thesis. If the null histogram is not flat, the test is wrong before any correction is applied — a hidden batch structure, a dependence the test ignores, or the wrong exchangeability assumption.

7. How significance is manufactured: p-hacking, forking paths and HARKing

None of the machinery above protects against the most common source of false findings, which is not a wrong formula but an unregistered analytic freedom. Three named versions:

  • p-hacking: trying analyses until one is significant — dropping outliers, adding a covariate, switching tests, collecting more data until p dips below 0.05[20]. The published literature shows the footprint of this practice as an excess of p-values just below 0.05[21].
  • The garden of forking paths[22]: the same inflation without any dishonesty, because the analysis choices were made after seeing the data, so the test that was eventually run was one of many that could have been run.
  • HARKing[23]: presenting a hypothesis formulated after the results as if it had been stated in advance, which converts an exploratory finding into a confirmatory claim it has not earned.

The simulation below quantifies the second one on a dataset in which, by construction, there is nothing to find.

forking_paths <- function(seed) {
  set.seed(seed)
  x <- rnorm(60); grp <- rep(0:1, each = 30); cov <- rnorm(60)   ## no effect whatsoever
  c(t.test(x[grp == 0], x[grp == 1], var.equal = TRUE)$p.value,            ## 1 plain t
    t.test(x[grp == 0], x[grp == 1])$p.value,                             ## 2 Welch
    suppressWarnings(wilcox.test(x[grp == 0], x[grp == 1])$p.value),      ## 3 rank test
    { k <- abs(x - mean(x)) < 2 * sd(x)                                   ## 4 drop 'outliers'
      t.test(x[k & grp == 0], x[k & grp == 1])$p.value },
    t.test(x[grp == 0 & cov > 0],  x[grp == 1 & cov > 0])$p.value,        ## 5 subgroup
    t.test(x[grp == 0 & cov <= 0], x[grp == 1 & cov <= 0])$p.value,       ## 6 other subgroup
    t.test(log1p(abs(x[grp == 0])), log1p(abs(x[grp == 1])))$p.value,     ## 7 transform
    t.test(x[grp == 0][1:20], x[grp == 1][1:20])$p.value,                 ## 8 stop early
    var.test(x[grp == 0], x[grp == 1])$p.value,                           ## 9 test the variance
    suppressWarnings(ks.test(x[grp == 0], x[grp == 1])$p.value))          ## 10 test the distribution
}
P <- t(sapply(1:2000, forking_paths))
best <- apply(P, 1, min); single <- P[, 1]
dd <- rbind(data.table(p = single, what = "pre-specified test only"),
            data.table(p = best,   what = "smallest of 10 analyses"))
p <- ggplot(dd, aes(p, fill = what)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, alpha = 0.7, position = "identity") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0.05, linetype = 2) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = unname(PAL[c("blue", "orange")]), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "p-value reported", y = "simulated studies",
       title = "Ten defensible choices turn a 5 % error rate into something else")
print(p)

cat("true effect in these data: ZERO\n")
## true effect in these data: ZERO
cat(sprintf("false-positive rate, pre-specified single test : %.1f %%\n", 100 * mean(single < 0.05)))
## false-positive rate, pre-specified single test : 4.4 %
cat(sprintf("false-positive rate, reporting the best of 10  : %.1f %%\n", 100 * mean(best < 0.05)))
## false-positive rate, reporting the best of 10  : 22.4 %
cat(sprintf("median reported p-value, best of 10            : %.3f\n", median(best)))
## median reported p-value, best of 10            : 0.135

Figure 9. Distribution of the reported p-value over 2,000 simulated studies in which the true effect is exactly zero. Reporting a single pre-specified test (blue) gives the correct error rate, 4.4 % here. Reporting the smallest p-value among ten analyses that any referee would accept as reasonable (orange) raises it to 22.4 % — one study in four or five — and no individual step in that process is fraudulent; the median reported p-value falls to 0.135. The forking-path inflation is a property of the procedure, which is why only pre-specification or an explicit multiplicity correction over the whole garden can control it.

A pre-registered analysis plan for a thesis chapter

Written before the data are looked at, half a page, in the thesis repository with a commit date:

  1. Question and primary endpoint. One sentence, one number. “Does scaffold series A have higher median pActivity than series B?”
  2. Data and exclusions. Which rows, which filters, and the exclusion rules — decided now, not after seeing which exclusions help.
  3. Primary analysis. The test, the effect size, the α, one-sided or two-sided, and the software.
  4. Multiplicity. How many hypotheses belong to the family, and which correction.
  5. Sample size / power. The effect size worth detecting and the n or number of replicas it requires (§8).
  6. Everything else is exploratory, and will be labelled as such in the text. Exploratory findings are hypotheses for the next experiment, not conclusions.

This is cheap, it protects the student rather than constraining them, and the practice is now standard in several fields[24][25].

8. Power: deciding how many replicas or compounds you need

Power is the probability that the test rejects the null when a specified effect really exists. It depends on the effect size, the variability, the sample size and α — fix any three and the fourth follows. A study with low power is not merely likely to miss a real effect; its significant results are also less likely to be true and are systematically exaggerated[26][27].

Closed-form power formulas exist for the t-test — power.t.test() in base R — but simulation is more general and far harder to get wrong: generate data under the alternative you care about, run your actual analysis pipeline, count the rejections.

sd_between <- sd(c(A - mean(A), B - mean(B)))       ## between-replica SD at fixed temperature
power_sim <- function(n, delta, sdv, nsim = 4000, alpha = 0.05, seed = 0) {
  set.seed(seed)
  x <- matrix(rnorm(nsim * n, 0, sdv), nrow = nsim)
  z <- matrix(rnorm(nsim * n, delta, sdv), nrow = nsim)
  v1 <- apply(x, 1, var); v2 <- apply(z, 1, var)
  se <- sqrt(v1 / n + v2 / n)
  dfw <- (v1 / n + v2 / n)^2 / ((v1 / n)^2 / (n - 1) + (v2 / n)^2 / (n - 1))
  mean(2 * pt(-abs((rowMeans(x) - rowMeans(z)) / se), df = dfw) < alpha)
}
deltas <- seq(0, 0.20, by = 0.01)
curves <- rbindlist(lapply(c(3, 5, 10, 20), function(n)
  data.table(n = factor(n), delta = deltas,
             power = sapply(deltas, function(d) power_sim(n, d, sd_between, seed = n)))))
p <- ggplot(curves, aes(delta, power, colour = n)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.8, linetype = 2) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = abs(mean(A) - mean(B)), linetype = 3) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = unname(PAL), name = "replicas\nper condition") +
  labs(x = "true difference in mean C-alpha RMSD (nm)", y = "power at alpha = 0.05",
       title = "Three replicas cannot see anything smaller than the replica spread")
print(p)

cat(sprintf("between-replica SD at fixed temperature: %.4f nm | observed difference %.4f nm\n",
            sd_between, abs(mean(A) - mean(B))))
## between-replica SD at fixed temperature: 0.0502 nm | observed difference 0.0203 nm
for (n in c(3, 5, 10, 20))
  cat(sprintf("  n = %2d replicas: power for 0.02 nm %.3f | 0.05 nm %.3f | 0.10 nm %.3f | 0.15 nm %.3f\n",
              n, power_sim(n, 0.02, sd_between, seed = n), power_sim(n, 0.05, sd_between, seed = n),
              power_sim(n, 0.10, sd_between, seed = n), power_sim(n, 0.15, sd_between, seed = n)))
##   n =  3 replicas: power for 0.02 nm 0.042 | 0.05 nm 0.112 | 0.10 nm 0.372 | 0.15 nm 0.664
##   n =  5 replicas: power for 0.02 nm 0.066 | 0.05 nm 0.252 | 0.10 nm 0.755 | 0.15 nm 0.982
##   n = 10 replicas: power for 0.02 nm 0.134 | 0.05 nm 0.554 | 0.10 nm 0.985 | 0.15 nm 1.000
##   n = 20 replicas: power for 0.02 nm 0.218 | 0.05 nm 0.856 | 0.10 nm 1.000 | 0.15 nm 1.000

Figure 10. Power curves for the temperature comparison, using the measured between-replica standard deviation of 0.0502 nm. With the three replicas we actually ran, the power to detect the difference we actually observed (dotted vertical line at 0.0203 nm) is 4.2 % — indistinguishable from the false-positive rate, which is another way of saying the experiment was blind to this effect. Three replicas reach 66 % power only at 0.15 nm, seven times the observed difference; ten replicas reach 98.5 % power at 0.10 nm and 55 % at 0.05 nm; twenty replicas reach 86 % at 0.05 nm. At the observed difference of 0.02 nm the four designs reach only 4.2 %, 6.6 %, 13.4 % and 21.8 % power respectively, which is the quantitative version of “this experiment could not have seen it”.

This calculation should be run before the simulations, not after, and it is the quantitative answer to the referee question “why three replicas?”. The honest answer in this dataset is that three replicas were chosen for teaching and for compute budget, and that the correct conclusion from them is “no detectable difference at 1 ns”, not “no difference”.

The same machinery sizes a chemistry experiment, and here the closed form is enough.

sd_pool <- sqrt((var(s1) + var(s2)) / 2)
ns <- seq(5, 400, by = 5)
pw <- rbindlist(lapply(c(0.2, 0.3, 0.5, 1.0), function(delta)
  data.table(delta = factor(sprintf("%.1f log units", delta)), n = ns,
             power = sapply(ns, function(n) power.t.test(n = n, delta = delta, sd = sd_pool,
                                                         sig.level = 0.05)$power))))
p <- ggplot(pw, aes(n, power, colour = delta)) +
  geom_line() + geom_hline(yintercept = 0.8, linetype = 2) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = unname(PAL), name = "true difference") +
  labs(x = "compounds per series", y = "power at alpha = 0.05",
       title = "Detecting a potency difference between two series")
print(p)

cat(sprintf("pooled SD of pActivity within a series: %.3f log units\n", sd_pool))
## pooled SD of pActivity within a series: 0.913 log units
for (delta in c(0.2, 0.3, 0.5, 1.0))
  cat(sprintf("  to detect %.1f log units with 80%% power: %5.0f compounds per series\n",
              delta, ceiling(power.t.test(delta = delta, sd = sd_pool, power = 0.8, sig.level = 0.05)$n)))
##   to detect 0.2 log units with 80% power:   328 compounds per series
##   to detect 0.3 log units with 80% power:   147 compounds per series
##   to detect 0.5 log units with 80% power:    54 compounds per series
##   to detect 1.0 log units with 80% power:    15 compounds per series
cat(sprintf("series actually available: S1 n = %d, S2 n = %d\n", length(s1), length(s2)))
## series actually available: S1 n = 207, S2 n = 59

Figure 11. Power against series size for four true potency differences, at the pooled within-series standard deviation of 0.913 log units measured in our own data. Detecting a 0.3-log difference — roughly a factor of two in IC50, the smallest difference a medicinal chemist would act on — needs 147 compounds per series at 80 % power, and a 0.2-log difference needs 328. Our second-largest series has 59 members, so a comparison involving it is powered only for differences of about half a log unit (54 compounds) and above. A one-log-unit difference needs only 15 compounds per side, which is why “series A is ten times more potent” is a claim small datasets can support and “series A is twice as potent” usually is not.

8.1 The winner’s curse

Low power does not only cause misses. Among the comparisons that do reach significance in an underpowered study, the estimated effects are systematically too large, because only the luckiest samples cross the threshold. This is the winner’s curse, and it explains a large part of why effect sizes shrink on replication.

true_delta <- 0.30; sd_w <- 0.90          ## a real 0.3-log difference, within-series SD as measured
wc <- rbindlist(lapply(c(10, 20, 40, 80, 160, 320), function(n) {
  set.seed(n)
  a <- matrix(rnorm(3000 * n, true_delta, sd_w), nrow = 3000)
  b <- matrix(rnorm(3000 * n, 0, sd_w), nrow = 3000)
  est <- rowMeans(a) - rowMeans(b)
  v1 <- apply(a, 1, var); v2 <- apply(b, 1, var); se <- sqrt(v1 / n + v2 / n)
  dfw <- (v1 / n + v2 / n)^2 / ((v1 / n)^2 / (n - 1) + (v2 / n)^2 / (n - 1))
  sig <- 2 * pt(-abs(est / se), df = dfw) < 0.05
  data.table(n_per_group = n, power = mean(sig), all_studies = mean(est),
             significant_only = mean(est[sig]), inflation = mean(est[sig]) / true_delta,
             sign_errors = mean(est[sig] < 0))
}))
p <- ggplot(melt(wc[, .(n_per_group, all_studies, significant_only)], id.vars = "n_per_group"),
            aes(n_per_group, value, colour = variable)) +
  geom_line() + geom_point(size = 1.6) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = true_delta, linetype = 2) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  scale_colour_manual(values = unname(PAL[c("blue", "orange")]), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "compounds per series", y = "estimated difference (log units)",
       title = "The winner's curse: small significant studies exaggerate")
print(p)

knitr::kable(wc, digits = 3)
n_per_group power all_studies significant_only inflation sign_errors
10 0.108 0.308 0.909 3.029 0.028
20 0.192 0.313 0.712 2.373 0.003
40 0.303 0.293 0.525 1.750 0.000
80 0.553 0.303 0.404 1.348 0.000
160 0.842 0.299 0.328 1.092 0.000
320 0.988 0.300 0.302 1.006 0.000

Figure 12. Simulated studies of a real 0.3-log effect (dashed line). Averaged over all studies (blue) the estimate is unbiased at every sample size, 0.293 to 0.313. Averaged over only the studies that reached p < 0.05 (orange) — the ones that would be published — the estimate is 0.909 at n = 10, an inflation factor of 3.0, and is still inflated by 35 % at n = 80, converging to the truth only once power exceeds 0.8. The last column of the table shows the darker consequence: in the smallest studies 2.8 % of the “significant” results have the wrong sign.

The practical consequences are immediate: never take an effect size from a small significant study as the input to your own power calculation (it is biased upwards, so your study will be underpowered), and treat a surprisingly large effect in a small sample as a reason for replication rather than for celebration.

9. The centrepiece: frame level versus replica level

Everything in this unit now converges on one experiment. We ask a single question — is the C-alpha RMSD of the Trp-cage different at 340 K than at 300 K after 1 ns? — and answer it twice with the same data: once treating each saved frame as an observation (1,500 per condition) and once treating each replica as an observation (three per condition).

frames_A <- md_obs[condition == "A", rmsd_ca_nm]
frames_B <- md_obs[condition == "B", rmsd_ca_nm]
t_frame <- t.test(frames_A, frames_B)
u_frame <- suppressWarnings(wilcox.test(frames_A, frames_B))
t_rep   <- t.test(A, B)
verdict <- data.table(
  unit = c("frame", "frame", "replica", "replica"),
  n_per_group = c(length(frames_A), length(frames_A), 3L, 3L),
  difference_nm = c(rep(mean(frames_A) - mean(frames_B), 2), rep(mean(A) - mean(B), 2)),
  test = c("Welch t", "Mann-Whitney", "Welch t", "permutation (exact, 20 splits)"),
  p = c(pfmt(t_frame$p.value), pfmt(u_frame$p.value), sprintf("%.3f", t_rep$p.value),
        sprintf("%.3f", p_exact)))
md_plot <- copy(md_obs)
md_plot[, xpos := ifelse(condition == "A", 1, 2) + (replica - 2) * 0.22]
set.seed(14)
md_plot[, xjit := xpos + rnorm(.N, 0, 0.02)]
p <- ggplot(md_plot, aes(xjit, rmsd_ca_nm, colour = condition)) +
  geom_point(size = 0.15, alpha = 0.25) +
  geom_point(data = md_plot[, .(xpos = xpos[1], rmsd_ca_nm = mean(rmsd_ca_nm)), by = .(condition, replica)],
             aes(xpos, rmsd_ca_nm), size = 2.6, shape = 21, fill = "white", stroke = 1.1) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(1, 2), labels = c("300 K (3 replicas)", "340 K (3 replicas)")) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = unname(PAL[c("blue", "orange")]), guide = "none") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "C-alpha RMSD (nm)",
       title = "Frames are many and dependent; replicas are few and independent")
print(p)

cat(sprintf("frame-level  : mean A %.4f vs B %.4f nm, Welch t = %.2f, p = %.3e\n",
            mean(frames_A), mean(frames_B), t_frame$statistic, t_frame$p.value))
## frame-level  : mean A 0.1736 vs B 0.1533 nm, Welch t = 10.81, p = 1.142e-26
cat(sprintf("replica-level: mean A %.4f vs B %.4f nm, Welch t = %.3f, p = %.3f (df %.2f)\n",
            mean(A), mean(B), t_rep$statistic, t_rep$p.value, t_rep$parameter))
## replica-level: mean A 0.1736 vs B 0.1533 nm, Welch t = 0.443, p = 0.690 (df 2.84)
cat(sprintf("ratio of p-values: %.1e\n", t_frame$p.value / t_rep$p.value))
## ratio of p-values: 1.7e-26
knitr::kable(verdict)
unit n_per_group difference_nm test p
frame 1500 0.0202962 Welch t 1.14e-26
frame 1500 0.0202962 Mann-Whitney 4.82e-13
replica 3 0.0202962 Welch t 0.690
replica 3 0.0202962 permutation (exact, 20 splits) 0.800

Figure 13. Every frame of all six runs (small dots) with the six replica means as open circles. The two conditions overlap almost completely, and the separation within condition A — whose three replicas average 0.110, 0.160 and 0.252 nm — is larger than the separation between the conditions (0.1736 against 0.1533 nm). The frame-level cloud is dense because frames are plentiful, not because the quantity is precisely known.

The table reports the two verdicts. At frame level the Welch test gives t = 10.81 and p = 1.14 × 10−26, and the Mann–Whitney test agrees at 4.8 × 10−13; at replica level the same comparison gives t = 0.443 and p = 0.690, and the exact permutation test gives 0.800 and could not have gone below 0.10 whatever happened. The two p-values differ by a factor of 1.7 × 10−26. The frame-level p-value is not a stronger version of the replica-level one; it is an answer to a different and uninteresting question — “do these 3,000 particular correlated numbers come from the same distribution?” — obtained by treating 3,000 dependent observations as 3,000 independent experiments. This is pseudoreplication[28], documented as a pervasive error in neuroscience[29] and equally common in simulation papers, where it is produced by the simple act of pasting a trajectory into a t-test.

obs_cols <- c("temperature_K", "box_volume_nm3", "rg_nm", "n_hbonds", "helix_fraction", "dist_W6_P12_nm")
both <- rbindlist(lapply(obs_cols, function(v) {
  pr <- md_obs[, .(m = mean(get(v))), by = .(condition, replica)]
  a <- pr[condition == "A", m]; b <- pr[condition == "B", m]
  data.table(observable = v, mean_A = mean(a), mean_B = mean(b),
             p_replica = t.test(a, b)$p.value,
             p_frame = t.test(md_obs[condition == "A", get(v)], md_obs[condition == "B", get(v)])$p.value)
}))
both[, holm_replica := p.adjust(p_replica, "holm")]
both[, `:=`(mean_A = signif(mean_A, 5), mean_B = signif(mean_B, 5),
            p_replica = signif(p_replica, 3), p_frame = signif(p_frame, 3),
            holm_replica = signif(holm_replica, 3))]
knitr::kable(both)
observable mean_A mean_B p_replica p_frame holm_replica
temperature_K 300.42000 340.24000 5.80e-06 0.000 2.88e-05
box_volume_nm3 47.76300 48.83700 5.00e-07 0.000 2.70e-06
rg_nm 0.69096 0.69025 8.76e-01 0.092 1.00e+00
n_hbonds 8.69930 9.05330 5.98e-01 0.000 1.00e+00
helix_fraction 0.88219 0.91743 5.44e-01 0.000 1.00e+00
dist_W6_P12_nm 0.59845 0.58008 3.61e-01 0.000 1.00e+00

Six observables, two units of analysis. The two control observables — temperature and box volume — separate the conditions at replica level with p = 5.8 × 10−6 and 4.6 × 10−7, surviving a Holm correction over the six tests, because a thermostat has almost no between-replica variance: the simulations did what they were told. Not one structural observable (radius of gyration, hydrogen bonds, helix fraction, cage distance) differs detectably at replica level, with p-values from 0.36 to 0.88. At frame level, by contrast, four of them look overwhelmingly significant — the helix fraction reaches 2.6 × 10−26 and the cage distance 2.4 × 10−30 — which is the same illusion as in Figure 13, repeated four times.

Three honest statements can be made about this dataset, and none of them is “340 K destabilises the protein”:

  1. The thermostat and barostat worked: temperature (300.42 K versus 340.24 K) and box volume (47.76 versus 48.84 nm³) separate the conditions at replica level.
  2. No structural observable differs detectably at 1 ns.
  3. The design had essentially no power to detect a difference of the size observed (§8), so statement 2 is “not detected”, not “not there”. Trp-cage unfolds on microsecond timescales, so a 1 ns window is not expected to show it.

The rule for simulation statistics

Identify the experimental unit before choosing a test. For molecular dynamics it is the independent run, not the frame[31]; for a clinical study with several samples per patient it is the patient; for a plate-based assay it is often the plate. If you have three units you have n = 3, and the correct report is an estimate with its between-unit interval plus an explicit statement of what effect size the design could have detected. If the frames must be used — for example to estimate an equilibrium average — then the autocorrelation correction of Unit 7 applies, and a mixed-effects model (Unit 9, Unit 10) is the principled way to use both levels at once.

10. Choosing a test, in practice

Decision sequence

  1. What is the experimental unit? Count those, not the measurements. If n is below about 6, prefer an exact permutation test and check whether significance is even attainable.
  2. Is the design paired? If there is a natural partner for each observation, use it — the gain usually exceeds anything the choice of test provides.
  3. What statistic answers the scientific question? Means, medians, proportions, ranks, an AUC. Write the effect size first, then pick the test that matches it.
  4. Check the assumptions that matter. Independence always; equal variances only for Student and ANOVA (R’s t.test defaults to Welch, and you should leave it there); normality mainly for small n (for large n the CLT covers means, as Unit 7 showed).
  5. Count the family. How many hypotheses could have been tested? Correct with Holm if a single false claim is costly, with BH if the output is a list of leads.
  6. Report the effect size with its interval, the n, the test, the correction and the power. The p-value is the least informative of these and should never travel alone[32].

The two-page “Points of Significance” columns in Nature Methods are an excellent companion to this checklist, in particular those on significance and t-tests[33] and on power and sample size[34]. All computations here used base R’s stats[1], car[36] and effectsize[35], on data curated from ChEMBL[30] and from a public gingival-tissue expression series[2].

Exercise 2

The last chunk tested six observables at both levels. Extend it: add the exact permutation p-value (all 20 labellings) for each observable at replica level, and a Cliff’s delta with its interval at frame level. Then answer in writing: which observables separate the conditions at replica level, why exactly those ones, and what the frame-level p-values of the other four are evidence of? Finally, re-run the whole table using only the last 500 ps of each trajectory and say whether any conclusion changes.

Bridge

This unit sits between Unit 7, which built the sampling distributions and intervals that every test here manipulates, and Unit 9, where a t-test becomes a test on a regression coefficient, an ANOVA becomes a linear model with categorical predictors, and the paired design becomes a blocking factor. Unit 10 answers the question a p-value cannot. The Python counterpart of this unit is here and the R edition is indexed at the course root. Forward, Unit 12 applies permutation testing to model metrics as y-randomisation and compares two models with paired tests; Unit 20 develops the replica statistics of §9 in full; Unit 21 scales §6 to a whole transcriptome with moderated tests. In the sister courses, the bioinformatics unit on molecular dynamics produces the trajectories analysed here, the one on molecular docking produces the ranked lists whose enrichment §2 tests, and the cheminformatics unit on validation uses the same permutation machinery on model scores.

11. Summary

You should be able to explain, without notes:

  • the four components of a test, and how to build a null distribution by permutation for any statistic;
  • why the classical tests are shortcuts of the permutation test, and which assumption each one buys its shortcut with;
  • why Welch’s test is R’s default and a better choice than Student’s (here t = 55 against a misleading 137), and why pairing is worth more than any choice of test;
  • what a p-value is, the four things it is not, and that a test and a confidence interval are the same statement;
  • how to compute and report Cohen’s d, Hedges’ g, Cliff’s delta and an odds ratio with intervals, and how to translate them into the units of the field;
  • the difference between family-wise error and false discovery rate, how the BH procedure works line by line, and why a p-value histogram must be inspected before correcting;
  • how a null comparison (healthy versus healthy, 8 raw hits and none surviving correction) validates an entire multiplicity pipeline;
  • how the garden of forking paths inflates a 4.4 % error rate to 22.4 % without any dishonesty, and what a pre-registered analysis plan contains;
  • how to estimate power by simulation, that 147 compounds per series are needed for a 0.3-log difference, and why significant small studies exaggerate by a factor of three;
