  • why the experimental unit, not the number of measurements, determines n — and that getting it wrong moved a p-value by 26 orders of magnitude.

12. Self-assessment

  1. Your permutation test with 1,000 shuffles reports p = 0. What do you write in the paper?
“p < 0.001 (1,000 permutations)”. A Monte-Carlo p-value is computed as (1 + number of shuffles at least as extreme)/(B + 1), so it can never legitimately be zero; the resolution of the test is 1/(B + 1), which was 0.0002 for the 5,000 permutations of §2.
  1. Three replicas per condition. What is the smallest two-sided p-value an exact permutation test can produce?
2/20 = 0.10, because there are only choose(6,3) = 20 ways to label six values as 3 + 3 and the observed labelling plus its mirror image are always at least as extreme as themselves. The design cannot reach 0.05 no matter what the data show.
  1. When should you use Student’s t-test rather than Welch’s?
Almost never, which is why t.test() in R defaults to Welch and you must write var.equal = TRUE to get Student’s. Welch’s test costs essentially nothing in power when the variances are equal and protects the error rate when they are not, particularly with unequal group sizes — in §3 the variance ratio was 24 and the two statistics differed by a factor of 2.5.
  1. A referee asks you to “add a non-parametric test because the data are not normal”. Is that a good reason?
Partly. Rank tests make fewer distributional assumptions but they answer a different question (stochastic ordering, not a difference of means) and they are not assumption-free — they still require independence, and the Wilcoxon signed-rank test assumes symmetric differences. With large samples the t-test on means is robust by the CLT; with small samples a permutation test on the statistic you actually care about is usually the better answer.
  1. You test 1,000 genes and 50 reach p < 0.05. Have you found anything?
Not yet: 50 is exactly what 1,000 true nulls would produce. Look at the p-value histogram (flat means nothing there), apply BH, and check whether any gene survives. In the null experiment of §6.1 eight genes reached raw p < 0.05 and none survived correction.
  1. What is the difference between controlling FWER and controlling FDR?
FWER is the probability of making at least one false rejection in the whole family; FDR is the expected proportion of false rejections among the rejections made. Controlling FWER is stricter and appropriate for confirmatory claims; controlling FDR is appropriate when the output is a ranked list of candidates for follow-up. Here BH kept 747 genes and Bonferroni 534.
  1. Your paired analysis gives p = 10⁻²⁰ and the unpaired analysis of the same data gives p = 10⁻¹⁷. Which do you report?
The paired one, because it matches the design: each diseased sample has a healthy partner from the same patient, and the unpaired test wastes that information by letting between-patient variation into the comparison. Report the design in the methods; a reader must be able to tell which test applies.
  1. Why is a result from a small, significant study a bad basis for a power calculation?
Because of the winner’s curse: among underpowered studies, only the ones whose estimate was luckily large reach significance, so the published effect is biased upwards — by a factor of 3.0 at n = 10 in the simulation of §8.1. Planning a new study on that inflated effect guarantees it will be underpowered too.
  1. How can a completely null dataset yield a significant result a fifth of the time?
If the analysis is chosen after seeing the data. Ten defensible analytic choices — a different test, an outlier rule, a subgroup, a transformation, stopping early — each with a 5 % false-positive rate and positively correlated with each other, give a 22.4 % chance that at least one is significant. Pre-specify the analysis, or correct over all the paths that were available.
  1. You have 3,000 MD frames and six runs. How many independent observations do you have?
Six, for any question about the difference between conditions. The frames within a run are autocorrelated (Unit 7 measured integrated autocorrelation times between about 18 and 80 ps), so they contribute a few dozen effectively independent samples each; but the quantity that varies between repetitions of the experiment is the run, so the run is the unit.
  1. The chi-square test and Fisher’s exact test disagree on your 2 × 2 table. Which do you trust?
Fisher’s, and the disagreement itself tells you why: the chi-square approximation degrades when expected cell counts fall below about 5. Check the expected counts (they are in chisq.test(tbl)$expected); if any is small, report the exact test and the odds ratio with its interval. In §3.2 the smallest expected count was 56, so the two agreed.
  1. Write the one-sentence result of the temperature comparison in this unit.
“Across three independent 1 ns replicas per condition, the mean C-alpha RMSD was 0.174 ± 0.042 nm at 300 K and 0.153 ± 0.020 nm at 340 K (Welch t-test on replica means, t = 0.44, p = 0.69; exact permutation p = 0.80); with this between-replica variability the design had 4 % power for the observed 0.02 nm difference, so no structural difference was detectable at this timescale.”

Glossary

Benjamini–Hochberg (BH)
Step-up procedure controlling the false discovery rate: reject the k smallest p-values where k is the largest rank with p(k) ≤ kα/m. p.adjust(p, “BH”).
Bonferroni correction
Test each of m hypotheses at α/m; controls the family-wise error rate, conservatively.
Cliff’s delta
Non-parametric effect size: P(X > Y) − P(X < Y), ranging from −1 to 1; algebraically the rank-biserial correlation.
Cohen’s d
Difference in means divided by the pooled standard deviation; Hedges’ g is its small-sample correction.
Effect size
A measure of how large a difference is, in units comparable across studies; always reported with an interval.
Exchangeability
The assumption that, under the null, the labels can be permuted without changing the joint distribution; it defines which permutation scheme is valid (label shuffle for independent groups, sign flip for pairs).
False discovery rate (FDR)
Expected proportion of false positives among rejected hypotheses.
Family-wise error rate (FWER)
Probability of at least one false positive in a family of tests.
Garden of forking paths
Inflation of the false-positive rate caused by data-dependent analysis choices, even without any deliberate searching.
HARKing
Hypothesising after the results are known, then presenting the hypothesis as pre-specified.
Holm procedure
Step-down FWER correction: uniformly more powerful than Bonferroni with the same guarantee.
Null hypothesis
A complete, simulatable description of “no effect”, against which the data are compared.
Odds ratio
Effect size for a 2 × 2 table: the ratio of the odds of an outcome in the two groups; its interval is built on the log scale.
Paired design
Each observation in one group has a natural partner in the other; analysis works on within-pair differences.
Permutation test
Null distribution built by relabelling the data; the general case of which the classical tests are shortcuts.
Power
Probability of rejecting the null when a specified effect is real; determined by effect size, variability, n and α. power.t.test() or simulation.
p-hacking
Searching analyses or stopping rules until a significant result appears.
Pseudoreplication
Treating repeated measurements of the same experimental unit as independent replicates.
q-value
The adjusted p-value of a BH-type procedure; the smallest FDR at which that hypothesis is rejected.
Rank-biserial correlation
Effect size derived from the Mann–Whitney statistic, 2U/(n₁n₂) − 1.
Welch’s t-test
Two-sample t-test that does not assume equal variances; the sensible default and R’s.
Winner’s curse
Upward bias of effect estimates among results selected for significance in underpowered studies.
